content:
President Trump traveled to San Antonio, Texas on Wednesday to campaign for Republican Texas Senate candidate Ken Paxton. The controversy continues to escalate after Trump made multiple remarks about Paxton's appearance.

The New York Times on September 30 released a leaked recording showing Paxton privately complaining that Trump's speech at a Republican midterm election rally in Dallas could affect his campaign. These remarks brought the issue back into the spotlight.

The President himself has yet to respond to the recording.

When campaigning for Paxton in Denton, Texas last week, Trump described Paxton as "sometimes really troublesome" and questioned whether he had attended the event (when in fact Paxton was present), before backtracking and calling him "the best Attorney General in the country."

On the final night of the Republican midterm election rally on September 10, Trump said: "I told him: 'Ken, I don't want to embarrass you, but we have too many disagreements... I'm not sure I like your look, I don't know if I like the way you dress, I don't like the way you talk.'"

The previous night, Trump had already said (Paxton) "might not dress neatly enough, might not give perfect speeches, and might not be the most handsome guy I've ever seen."

In early September, speaking from the Oval Office about Paxton's Democratic opponent James Talarico, Trump said: "We have a guy named Ken Paxton. Some people don't like the way he dresses, some people don't like the way he gives interviews, and some people don't like the way he talks."

With less than five weeks until the November midterms, the Texas Senate race remains tight. According to a latest poll by The New York Times and Siena College released on October 3, Paxton trails Talarico by six percentage points.

Trump's comments on Paxton's appearance appear to have become a recurring pattern.

Dan Cassino, a political science professor at Fairleigh Dickinson University, told The Huffington Post that Trump has consistently equated external masculine traits with strong leadership.

Cassino pointed out: "At the end of the day, the issue is that Trump has a very clear standard for what a good candidate should be and look like. In his mind, the ideal candidate is male, tall, handsome, and dresses according to his own preferences. If you don't meet this model, or fall short of this stereotype in any way, Trump will consider you an unqualified candidate."

Trump also frequently comments on his own appearance. Speaking in Nebraska on Monday, he claimed supporters told him he looked in great shape, with more presidential bearing than former presidents George Washington and Abraham Lincoln.

During his first presidential term in 2016, he once asked the crowd: "I think I have a very strong presidential aura. Do I look like a president? I think I look like a president... Am I very handsome?"

Cassino said: "When Trump endorses someone or campaigns alongside them, and that person doesn't meet his standards, this mindset becomes a problem. His comments (about Paxton) reflect his belief that Paxton isn't masculine enough, and therefore doesn't look like a good candidate, nor someone who can win."

Is Trump intentionally making these remarks about Paxton?

Brandon Rottinghaus, a political science professor at the University of Houston, believes Trump may be laying the groundwork in case Paxton loses.

Rottinghaus pointed out: "At the end of the day, the question is: who takes responsibility? The President may be creating a situation where Paxton has to bear full responsibility for a possible defeat in the state. Trump doesn't want to be the person everyone points to as the cause of Republican election losses."

However, Rottinghaus emphasized this is only his personal speculation.

He said: "The President's strategy has always been hard to pin down, because he tends to speak casually on these issues. Paxton needs Trump's endorsement and support, and Trump is also happy to make Paxton a laughingstock."

Josh Blank, director of the Texas Politics Project at the University of Texas at Austin, offered two other interpretations. The first is that these remarks may simply reflect his displeasure with the trouble Paxton has caused for the Republicans.

Blank told The Huffington Post: "If the President is overly focused on Ken Paxton's negative traits, it may just be a venting of frustration."

Another possibility is that these remarks give voters a harmless, trivial flaw to focus on, "allowing voters to continue supporting him while also excusing themselves and acknowledging his shortcomings."

Paxton has faced multiple charges throughout his political career, including securities fraud, corruption, bribery, abuse of power, and retaliation against whistleblowers. Blank also noted that Paxton has consistently refused to debate Talarico.

Blank said: "This is not a normal election. If Republicans start acting strangely in the final months of the campaign, it's because they're not used to being in this position."

Carl Gilson, a political science professor at Southern Methodist University who specializes in Texas politics, believes Paxton's base will very likely continue to support him.

Speaking about Paxton, Gilson said: "I was chatting with an old friend yesterday, and he said: 'You know, he's a con artist, but he's our con artist.' That perfectly sums up how the Republican base feels."

Why does this election matter?

Paxton is extremely well-known in Texas. After ten years in the state legislature, he was elected Attorney General in 2014. Since 2016, he has been a steadfast supporter of the "Make America Great Again" (MAGA) movement, and has received millions of dollars in campaign donations through a new political action committee based in Texas and connected to Senate Majority Leader John Thune called "MAGA Inc.," as well as other Republican organizations.

Gilson pointed out that a loss would have deeper implications. "If Paxton loses, and the governor's race is also extremely, extremely tight, the consequences will be catastrophic."

As of publication, Paxton's team had not responded to The Huffington Post's interview request.

Zach Kraft, a spokesman for the Republican National Committee, replied to The Huffington Post's inquiry: "President Trump has already called Ken Paxton the greatest Attorney General ever, and made it clear that he will do everything in his power to help him become the next Texas U.S. Senator. As Texans learn more about James Talarico's radical agenda—eliminating the oil and gas industry, raising taxes, and forcing children into gender transitions—they will increasingly realize they absolutely don't want anything to do with this person."
